chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadeed, from Jameel, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Regarding the one who does not know whether he prayed three or four, and his imagination regarding that is equal, he said: 'When the imagination is equal between three and four, he has the choice: if he wishes, he prays one rak'ah while standing, and if he wishes, he prays two rak'ah and four prostrations while sitting.'

And he said regarding a man who does not know whether he prayed two or four, and his imagination goes towards four or towards two rak'ah, that he prays two rak'ah and four prostrations. And he said: 'If your imagination goes towards two and four, it is the same, and the imagination in this case is not like it in the case of three and four.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for prayer when one is unsure if they prayed three or four rak'ahs?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of *Shakk al-Mutabiq* (symmetrical doubt) in prayer, distinguishing between the flexibility allowed for uncertainty between three and four rak'ahs versus the stricter default of two rak'ahs for uncertainty between two and four. It highlights the scholarly principle that when doubt is equal, the worshipper may choose the easier path, yet notes that the specific mechanics of completion differ based on the base number of rak'ahs, reflecting the nuanced application of *Ihtiyat* (precaution) in Shia fiqh.
